title: Met to re-examine CCTV footage from unsolved Jill Dando murder
description: The TV presenter and newsreader was born in Weston-Super-Mare, Somerset, and worked for the BBC for 14 years. She was 37 when she died on the doorstep
body: The TV presenter and newsreader was born in Weston-Super-Mare, Somerset, and worked for the BBC for 14 years. She was 37 when she died on the doorstep of her home on Gowan Avenue.Soon after her death, a man of Serbian descent called the BBC claiming she had been executed in a revenge hit for the UK-backed Nato bombing of Serbia's state broadcaster in Belgrade.However, Barry George, a local man, was convicted of her murder and spent eight years in jail before being acquitted at a retrial in 2008. Dando's partner, Alan Farthing, was interviewed by the police, along with her ex-partner and BBC Breakfast news editor Bob Wheaton. Also interviewed was her agent Jon Roseman, who had written a crime novel detailing a very similar scene.They were all ruled out as suspects. Her killing was the subject of a Netflix documentary Who Killed Jill Dando? in 2023.Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

schema.headline: Met to re-examine CCTV footage from unsolved Jill Dando murder

title: Security lapses at Utah campus where Charlie Kirk was killed, review says
description: An independent review has pointed to a number of security shortcomings at the Utah campus where conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot dead last
body: An independent review has pointed to a number of security shortcomings at the Utah campus where conservative activist Charlie Kirk was shot dead last year.The report said Utah Valley University (UVU) did not carry out a proper written security assessment nor prepare an event action plan, deferring key decision-making about the event to Kirk's conservative organisation Turning Point USA.It also said that Kirk's aides had insisted on a outdoor venue, overriding security concerns from campus officials, who then failed to properly assess the dangers.The 31-year-old activist had been addressing thousands of people in an Orem campus courtyard when he was shot from a nearby rooftop on 10 September 2025.Kirk's family said the report reinforced their concerns about how the event was managed.University officials had raised concerns in August 2025 about holding the event at a location surrounded by tall buildings and had suggested alternative venues, including some indoors, the report, external - published by UVU - says. "But a Turning Point representative insisted that Kirk speak at a campus courtyard because he had been there previously and the organisation was familiar with the location," it adds. Despite the "significant protective operations considerations", no line-of-sight assessment was documented in the planning process, the external consultants note.They also identified shortcomings in the co-ordination between university police and Kirk's private security team. A proposed meeting between the university's police chief and Turning Point security shortly before the event did not take place, the report said. The reviewers described the absence of a joint security briefing and walk-through as a missed opportunity to have identified risks, clarified responsibilities and considered additional security measures. However, the review concluded that no university employee or representative had acted in bad faith or shown "willful and wanton disregard" for anyone's safety.Kirk's family has previously accused the university of serious security failures and has filed a wrongful-death notice, a step that can precede legal action.The family's lawyer, Brett Parkinson, said the independent report released on Friday backed up the concerns raised by Kirk's loved ones."The buck stopped with UVU leadership and law enforcement," Parkinson said in a statement to the Associated Press. "Justice for Charlie and his family requires true accountability for UVU's fatal shortcomings that day."When asked for comment on the findings, Turning Point USA referred to Parkinson's statement.The review makes numerous recommendations aimed at improving security for major campus events. UVU President Jon Anderson said the university must "learn from the findings of this review, and follow through on its recommendations".It has previously been reported that the campus police failed to conduct security procedures that are common practice at US high-profile events, including flying a drone to monitor rooftops or security screening like bag checks and metal detectors.Kirk had been debating UVU students about US mass shootings, as part of a series of events across different university campuses, when he was shot in the neck shortly after noon. He was rushed to hospital but later pronounced dead.His alleged killer, Tyler Robinson, has pleaded not guilty to aggravated murder in connection with Kirk's death. Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty.

schema.headline: Security lapses at Utah campus where Charlie Kirk was killed, review says

title: England 2-3 Spain: Thomas Tuchel rues 'big mistakes' - did Man City charges have impact?
description: Three City players - Elliot Anderson, Guehi and O'Reilly - started for England, while Rodri, who spent seven years at the club, was in Spain's XI.And
body: Three City players - Elliot Anderson, Guehi and O'Reilly - started for England, while Rodri, who spent seven years at the club, was in Spain's XI.And three of those four players made significant errors at Wembley.First Guehi was tackled by Lamine Yamal on the edge of his own box, allowing the Spain winger to drive towards goal and slot in his side's opener.In the second half Rodri's late challenge on Jude Bellingham led to an England penalty, which Harry Kane struck against the crossbar after slipping.And then O'Reilly had a pass intercepted deep in his own half which led to Alex Baena's equaliser at 2-2.On Friday, sources told BBC Sport City had been found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they were accused of breaching.After a four-year investigation, the club were accused of a wide range of rule breaches centring around claims they inflated sponsorship revenue and made other "off the books" payments to circumvent financial rules between 2009 and 2018.Sanctions are yet to be announced, but repercussions could include a points deduction, expulsion from the Premier League or a huge fine.BBC Sport understands Premier League clubs are seeking legal advice about potential compensation.England captain Kane played down any links between the charges and player mistakes, telling ITV Sport after Saturday's game: "There was a discussion, but at the end of the day when we're with England we kind of put club football to one side and it was no different this week."

schema.headline: England 2-3 Spain: Thomas Tuchel rues 'big mistakes' - did Man City charges have impact?

title: Classy or classist? How bare nails became a hot issue
description: In recent months, Paloma Buddemeier has watched a stream of people walk into her nail salon with the goal of looking as if they'd never been there at
body: In recent months, Paloma Buddemeier has watched a stream of people walk into her nail salon with the goal of looking as if they'd never been there at all."It's crazy," the owner of Wumman Spa in London says.These customers still get their nails filed, buffed, and trimmed. "You still do the cuticle, you do the soaking and hydrate everything," says Buddemeier, "but you just put no polish on."Driving this, she says, is a viral craze for bare-looking nails.In recent months, artsy shots of glossy naked nails have been flooding social media and taking over fashion runways and red carpets, which some are viewing as the latest symbol of "quiet luxury".But critics argue the bare nails trend actually says something about class, the hamster wheel of beauty standards, and who gets to define what is considered tasteful.Nail art's historical and creative roots are linked back to black, Latino, and Asian communities and the suggestion that bare nails are now a sign of high status could stigmatise bold manicures, they say."That trend really promotes blankness and this kind of sameness and erasure of culture and identity that is so important to black and brown communities," beauty journalist Kristina Rodulfo tells the BBC."They are often called elegant or tasteful, and these are often usually euphemisms that perpetuate white supremacist standards of beauty."For some, though, the choice is less about a dislike of bold nails and more about simplifying their routine.Some converts say they're ditching polish as a way of rebelling against an entrenched female beauty standard or to save time and money. Others just love the look. Then, there are some women who've long left their nails alone, amused to find their routine – or lack thereof – suddenly in vogue.For years, Irish TV presenter Angela Scanlon marched herself to a nail salon every fortnight, a routine that started when she was living in New York in the 2000s. There, she says, manicures were so universal they felt like a uniform. But it soon became a chore.Scanlon would have everything from thin, shiny shellac to sturdier "Builder In A Bottle" gel manicures layered onto her nails every other week without fail."It wasn't like I was in my head going: 'I must go because Dave from Hull is going to be disgusted if I'm on This Morning next week without a full set'," the Radio 2 presenter says. "I just added it to the list of things that we must do... in the way you would wash your hair."Eventually, in a moment of clarity, Scanlon decided to stop going, in a bid to free up time and mental bandwidth."I heard myself saying to people: 'Ugh, my god, I have to go and get my nails done.'"And I thought: 'I probably don't need to do this anymore'."Scanlon's posts about her decision to ditch the continuous manicure blew up on Substack and Instagram earlier this year. She seemed to have tapped into a vein.Simple nails were in the spotlight at New York Fashion Week in February, with Marc Jacobs among those sending his models out polish-less, though some fashionistas argue this is not new.But beauty magazines have declared "All The Cool Girls Are Quietly Quitting Manicures, external", that "Bare Nails Are the New Status Symbol, external" of "Polished Women" and that "Manicures Are No Longer Classy, external".And there's a never-ending stream of posts on Insta and TikTok promoting shiny, natural-looking nails, and detailing how you can get them yourself. The look has become so hyped some have gone full circle, booking in salon appointments to mimic it.At the Wumman Spa nail salon, some of Buddemeier's clients sit in the chair for hours, as nail artists build them hyper-realistic fake nails in sheer, glossy neutrals, à la Zoe Kravitz and Zendaya.Londoner Khadija says she was once a fan of elaborate nail art but pivoted to bare nails earlier this year."It's just really chic. And I love less is more, I love minimalism... less consumerism and just self-care things that you could probably do at home."Reluctantly joining the bandwagon thanks to the rising cost of living is her friend Emmanuella. "It's just too expensive now," she says."I think getting [your] nails done is tacky now, because who's got an hour to waste?" one 25-year-old tells the BBC, adding, "also, I lift weights in the gym, so I don't want to snap a nail and waste money."But there are those who think the trend - or the way it's being discussed by some - belies something more sinister.Manicures have been whispering messages about the wearer's position in society for as long as they have existed, according to fashion journalist Suzanne E. Shapiro."Women's bodies - and sense of self-presentation - have always held huge political and cultural significance," Shapiro, who wrote Nails: The Story of The Modern Manicure, tells the BBC.Even back in 13th century Imperial China, the lengthy talons grown by nobility and the delicately carved brass nail shields which usually guarded them were a symbol of a life unmarred by manual labour.A single layer of the rose-tinted waxy salves which were popular in the 1800s was a sign of vigour and health, but two layers - in an era when cosmetics and artificial beauty were tied to virtue - was the mark of a vain or "loose" woman.And the red at-home nail lacquer, released by Revlon in the early 1930s, was a badge of honour for modern women rebelling against that kind of oppressive judgement.But it was women of colour who really made manicures an accessible and fashionable form of self-expression, historians say.Entertainer Josephine Baker, disco icons Diana Ross and Donna Summer, and Olympic gold-medal-winning sprinter Florence Griffith-Joyner - whose dramatic acrylic sets often distracted headline writers from her record-setting performances - have all pioneered nail art.And when waves of Vietnamese refugees gave rise to the nail bar in the 1970s, professional manicures were no longer the preserve of the rich.But, like many luxuries, as they became more popular and more accessible to the masses, the wealthy began pivoting – a textbook example of behaviour known as "counter signalling", Rudolfo says."The same way that logo bags are considered gauche or quiet luxury is more aspirational, bare nails are considered the trend now."The examples are almost always white women or celebrities... [and] they'll often conflate class and taste with that bareness."Others point out bare nails often demand their own time-consuming and costly routine."The irony in all this is these natural nails are not natural either," Shapiro says. "They also require a lot of grooming and sometimes pretty premiere services."Few would argue there aren't valid feminist questions for the beauty industry to answer, around unrealistic standards for example, but the largely female-run nail sector also feels empowering for many women."I feel like nail care has very much had a 'for women, by women' sort of ethos around it," Shapiro says. "The first salon opened in New York City was owned by a woman, and she was a remarkably independent one... a lot of the first entrepreneurs offering product lines, opening salons were women."Hampton admits she's saddened by the way trends have been – and continue to be - weaponised."We're taking the fun out of nails... Anyone should be able to wear what they like - nail polish or bare nails," she says. "Why is there an argument? Why is there beef?"Scanlon too is a little baffled."For me, it's like, just stop judging ourselves and everybody else," she says. "Some people like to have the nails done, some people don't. "I suppose the question that I was posing was, is it doing anything for you?"The truth of it is: it's not that deep."

schema.headline: Classy or classist? How bare nails became a hot issue

title: Biao Xiang: Young people in China are fangirling over a professor who gets their anxiety
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Young Chinese people are anxious about their future in a rapdily changing countryByFan Wang"A star sent from
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Young Chinese people are anxious about their future in a rapdily changing countryByFan Wang"A star sent from the heavens," is how Zihan Han describes the man she's become a huge fan of recently, a man who young Chinese people call an "idol".Except this is no pop singer or movie star, but a 54-year old anthropologist. Professor Biao Xiang has become an unlikely guide for an increasingly disillusioned generation.And it's because of what he talks about: anxiety and how to navigate it.China's economy and tech have grown at breakneck speed, but there is plenty worrying its Gen Z, from jobs to romantic prospects to the sheer pressure of keeping up."The transition from school to the real world brings a lot of uncertainty now, and people often feel anxious because they don't know how to face it," says a 23-year-old Chinese graduate who didn't want to reveal her name because she was worried speaking to foreign media might affect her chances of finding a job back home."People need an anchor in their life. And his words make us feel there is someone that gets me."She and Zihan were among some 500 people - mostly Chinese diaspora - who piled into an auditorium recently in Singapore. Xiang spoke for more than an hour in Mandarin before he took questions. When it ended, dozens queued to meet and take photos with him. The Chinese grad called it "an academic fan meeting".Xiang has been interviewed by major Chinese outlets and has travelled to top Chinese campuses to talk, including at his alma mater, the prestigious Peking University – one talk earlier this year was live-streamed because the auditorium was full.  "When in doubt, ask Biao Xiang," has become a saying, according to Chinese media.Image caption, About 500 people heard Biao Xiang speak in Singapore recentlyIn Sinapore, Xiang spoke of the recognition young people seek in today's China, where they often look to systems for approval - from competitive exams to secure jobs - and how that approval becomes a measure of self-worth, which can be exhausting and damaging. It is healthier, he suggested, to seek meaning and understanding from others and use that to understand ourselves better.These are hardly quick fixes. But in a country where discontent can be politically sensitive and heavily censored, he is a rare public figure who addresses what he calls the "pain point of the times"."Everyone knows where the issue is, but they are reluctant to look at it. Sometimes it is too painful to look at, or they don't have a way," he tells the BBC over tea in Singapore."But as an academic, it is not terrifying if you can describe it – that's how you analyse and manage it."He now lives in Germany, where he is the director of the Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology, and studies social change in China and other parts of Asia.Xiang believes Chinese society is at a "turning point", where people are searching for meaning while making sense of rapid social and economic change. He sees contradictions – uncertain youth in a powerful, assertive country; disillusionment despite huge advancement – and his job, he says, is to unpack what is driving it.China's leader Xi Jinping has acknowledged it too: he said the "principal contradiction" was "between the people's ever-growing needs for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Young people are seeking a new narrative in a highly competitive China, Xiang says Xiang has catchy names for what is causing this. "Floating" is how he describes people working relentlessly just to survive, like a hummingbird that keeps flapping its wings to stay mid-air."The nearby" refers to what is immediately around us. Xiang argues that people are preoccupied by the "very near" (themselves) and the very far (the world) while the space in between - "the nearby" - is neglected. This, he says, leaves them feeling disconnected.This seems to be resonating deeply with young people looking for answers. One user on RedNote writes, "He consistently views issues from the perspective of the vulnerable, attributes personal stress to macro-level causes, and encourages people to actively engage with life - it's truly wonderful."Another says, "He never spouts empty, feel-good platitudes; instead, he crouches down to face real-life dilemmas alongside us."Zihan says it boils down to Xiang's willingness to talk openly about these things: "Those who have said similar things aren't as kick-ass as Teacher Xiang, yet people who are as kick-ass as him haven't said such things."Image caption, Xiang has become famous among Chinese people for his candid lecturesBorn in 1972, Xiang came of age during another turning point, as China emerged from the brutal chaos of Mao Zedong's rule to trade with the world. It urbanised, ordinary people turned into entrepreneurs and businesses took off for the first time in the Communist nation.Growing up in Wenzhou, which transformed into an industrial port, Xiang witnessed this first-hand. "It was a vast landscape of small business owners," he recalls. "Most people didn't care too much about education, the focus was on practical matters - specifically, how to make money."And many of them did. Their children grew up in a glorious era of double-digit economic growth. But the economy slowed during Covid and hasn't bounced back. The old equation - hard work = secure job - no longer works, and they want a new narrative, Xiang says.Youth unemployment hit 21.3%, before the government stopped publishing the data in mid-2023. Those with "good jobs" - civil servants, corporate employees, engineers - are anxious about losing them.They constantly complain online about long, exhausting working hours and a toxic office culture and their fear of the "curse of 35" - a cutoff age for job advertisements, after which it is harder to find a new job.Because of censorship, it's hard to know the true extent of this mood. But that feeling of being squeezed seeps into public discourse in other ways. That anxiety quickly turns into anger in online debates, be it about university entrance exams or bride price or food safety scandals.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Young people praying at monastery in Beijing for bright job and marriage prospects   Terms associated with this mood have been trending for years. The most famous are "lying flat", when people opt out of the rat race entirely, and "involution", a rather clunky term now commonly used to describe intense competition which generates little meaningful reward.Xiang believes two forces have amplified this anxiety - the property market and the higher education system. The property boom, fuelled by local government's reliance on land sales, tied families' sense of security and success to the values of their homes. And a rapid expansion in university enrolment raised the bar for achievement, intensifying competition.The result, he says, is a universal playbook: get a good degree, find a stable job, marry and buy a home."When 1.4 billion people are all in the same race, that is involution."About three years ago, when he learned that a camp for digital nomads where he spoke raised prices after his visit, he "realised I was no longer only known in the academic circles".Many of his peers, he said, prioritise publishing research and are "quite cold" to his methods. Some warned him about "cherishing your feathers", a Chinese expression for protecting one's reputation.But Xiang is encouraged by his popularity."If someone calls me an influencer I'll take it as a compliment. Because the real influence I can have is to make people think for themselves."

schema.headline: Biao Xiang: Young people in China are fangirling over a professor who gets their anxiety

title: Keep dancing: 100-year-old leads Worcester charity flash mob
description: A 100-year-old man, already known for his dance moves through social media, led a flash mob with hundreds of people joining in.Wearing a bright red sh
body: A 100-year-old man, already known for his dance moves through social media, led a flash mob with hundreds of people joining in.Wearing a bright red shirt, Bernard Gilbert directed a dance to song King of the Road by country singer Roger Miller in Worcester city centre, with crowds erupting in applause after he finished.The former dance teacher previously went viral on social media for his moves at Fernhill House Care Home where he lives. His videos were seen more than 1.5m times."I love the dancing, once I get on the floor I forget everything, I just concentrate on what I'm doing," he said when the BBC interviewed him in June. The flash mob in Cathedral Square featured Got2Sing choir members as well as residents as they raised money for Alzheimer's Research UK. They learnt four dances, practised hard and rehearsed at home to prepare for the event, Fernhill House Care Home said."What an inspiring day, what a community, what a fantastic memory we've created together," it added.Organisers of Got2Sing Worcester described the flash mob as a "joyful afternoon" with singers "bringing their energy and talent" to the city centre."When a 100-year-old local legend leads the line dancing, you know it's going to be a good afternoon," they said.

schema.headline: Keep dancing: 100-year-old leads Worcester charity flash mob

title: Meet the pensioners spending the kids' inheritance
description: Happily retired, Sarah Moorhouse is using her private pension "to go places and do nice things at the drop of a hat".While other retirees with a decen
body: Happily retired, Sarah Moorhouse is using her private pension "to go places and do nice things at the drop of a hat".While other retirees with a decent monthly pension income may choose to build up an inheritance for their children, Sarah, 64, and her husband Geoff are opting to spend their money on living life to the max."We like going to Scotland," says Sarah, a retired school administrator. "We've been down to Cambridgeshire, which was lovely. We go up to the Lake District quite regularly to a holiday cottage, and we're planning to go to Norfolk."The couple, who live in the Yorkshire Dales, go on holiday four or five times a year, spending hundreds of pounds each time because, in Sarah's view, "you only have one opportunity at life". They did recently sell their vintage Sunbeam Alpine sports car. But only so they could replace it with a more modern, sporty two-seater convertible, a Mazda MX-5."I'm of an age where I'm going to friends' and acquaintances' funerals, and I think you just need to live life and enjoy it while you can, because it's a very precious commodity," says Sarah.Sarah and Geoff are part of a global personal finance phenomenon that has been dubbed "skiing", which stands for spending the kids' inheritance. It is challenging the notion that assets will get handed down to the next generation.One in seven UK parents of children of all ages (15%) now plan to prioritise enjoying their money in their retirement over leaving an inheritance, according to a March report, external by pension provider Standard Life. And in the US, the number of people expecting to get an inheritance from their parents dropped to 20% last year, from 25% in 2024, according to a study, external by financial services firm Northwestern Mutual. Sarah and Geoff have two adult daughters. One of them, Poppy, tells the BBC that she couldn't be happier that her parents are out and about having fun.She firmly rejects the notion that she and her sister should expect an inheritance. "To me that's wild. It never even crossed my mind that I'll get money when my mum and dad die. I'd so much rather them do what they want to do."Mike Ambery, retirement and savings director at Standard Life, believes that the move towards skiing in the UK has been driven by the disappearance of final-salary pensions, which provide guaranteed monthly pension payments that last for as long as the retiree lives.Instead, more people in the UK now have what are called defined contribution pension pots, which can run out. Ambery argues that it's easier to be generous with a legacy if you know your retirement income will last as long as you need it.He also points to pensioners wanting to simply enjoy themselves after a life of working. "It's just having a little bit of indulgence to enjoy life. Let's face it, working life can be very hard for some people."Not all retirees are well off, of course. In the UK, 16% of pensioners live in poverty, , externalaccording to the Joseph Rowntree Foundation charity. The figure for the US is 15.4%, newly released data shows., externalBut at the same time, UK pensioners have seen their disposable income, excluding housing costs, increase by more than that of non-pensioners over the last three decades, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies think tank, external.Originally from Berkshire, Karen has lived in Provence in the south of France for the past 11 years, and spends more than £10,000 a year on holidays."This year, I'm going to a yoga retreat. I did one in March in Morocco," she says. "Then in October into November I'm going to Vietnam and Laos to do a little bit of a tour."She describes herself as semi-retired, as she tops up her private pension by still doing some business consultancy work, the job she used to do full-time.When it comes to how much money she has per month, she says that her income is the same as when she was working full-time. In addition to her pension and income from her part-time work, she gains 40% of her funds from renting out a property.But Karen insists she's not "crazy with money" and likes "to get a deal".Like Sarah Moorhouse she won't get her UK state pension until she is 67. That's currently a standard £12,547.60 a year for people who reached the state pension age after April 2016, but it is due to go up next year.As a comparison, retirees in the US get state payments known as social security retirement benefits. The maximum annual amount starting from the "full retirement age" of 67 is $49,824 (£36,993)., external However, people can choose to take a lower payment, external from the age of 62.Matthew Loveless, a vice president at Northwestern Mutual, based in Ohio, says retirees need to be upfront with their adult children, some of whom might be expecting an inheritance that they intend to rely on.Back in Yorkshire, Sarah says that despite the spending, she has every intention of leaving her kids something. In the meantime she is planning her next holiday. "I've worked hard all my life and I think I deserve to have a bit of free time and to be able to do nice things."Additional reporting by Miguel Roca-Terry

schema.headline: Meet the pensioners spending the kids' inheritance

title: Israel v Republic of Ireland: Republic of Ireland to wear black armbands for Israel game
description: Republic of Ireland players intend to wear black armbands "in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict" for Sunday's Nations League game a
body: Republic of Ireland players intend to wear black armbands "in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict" for Sunday's Nations League game against Israel in Hungary, after confirming they will go ahead with the fixture.Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell confirmed one player has withdrawn from the squad before the match.But he added that a vote among the squad produced a "significant majority" in favour of playing.As well as the intention to wear black armbands for Sunday's 'away' game against Israel in Debrecen, Courell said the players will make further gestures for the initial game and the return 'home' fixture against Israel next Sunday in Serbia.The fixtures have been embroiled in controversy since the two teams were drawn to play each other in Group B3.Republic of Ireland players faced calls to withdraw from the games because of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war with a "Stop The Game" campaign - organised by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine - gathering pace."One of their requests is to remove their media obligations for the remainder of this window," Courell said at Saturday's delayed news conference."They also have the intention to wear black armbands in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict. "There will be elements of the pre-match ceremony not be partaken in by the Republic of Ireland and it is also the intention of the players to make a significant contribution to charitable donation by virtue of both [Israel] match fees and also the fixture against Austria at the Aviva [Stadium in Dublin on Thursday]."There appeared to be real doubt on Saturday morning whether the fixture would take place.A pre-match news conference with manager Heimir Hallgrimsson and a player, scheduled for 09:15 BST, was postponed just 15 minutes before it was scheduled to start, with reporters informed it would instead take place after the team's training session which was also delayed.The players were locked in a meeting back at their hotel after it emerged a player, goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, withdrew from the game in protest with several other expressing their concerns about fielding.About 13:00, players began to filter out of the meeting room, with it then confirmed the news conference would indeed go ahead, back at Nagyerdei Stadion at 14:30, with training to follow.More than five hours after the initial news conference was scheduled to begin, Courell - flanked by Hallgrimsson and FAI director of football John Martin - confirmed a players' vote passed by a "significant majority" to play the game."This morning, a player expressed their discomfort at the fixture and indicated their intent to withdraw," Courell said."This new variable required time for the rest of the squad to consider and what proceeded was another four hours of conversations, predominantly among the players, but also at times with coaching staff and the [FAI] executive."There were a lot of positions presented and the association is fully respectful of everyone's right to their respective opinion."Later on Saturday, Bazunu posted on social media explaining his decision, one that he said he had "not taken lightly"."I am a man of strong faith and try my best to be a person of character and principle, therefore I feel it would be wrong to participate in the upcoming fixtures against Israel," he said."My decision is based purely upon my personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong."It is important to note that my stance is not in opposition of the Israel people or the Jewish community but against the atrocities in the region."There are few times when you get a chance in life to stand up for something bigger and I strongly believe that this is one of them."Former Republic of Ireland manager Brian Kerr and ex-international James McClean are among those to have backed calls for a boycott of the fixtures.The armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.Hallgrimsson relayed that nobody "can understand the pressure that has been going on these players" and said the lengthy meeting on Saturday stemmed from "a change of mind for one of the players to play the game"."All of the rest of the players are training today," he confirmed."The balance [to play] changed with this [withdrawal] and obviously it was an ongoing discussion but we came to a conclusion and the game is going ahead."We will train and there will probably be more discussions tonight and probably tomorrow. It's a unique situation and we are just trying to limit the damage."The Republic of Ireland lost their opening Nations League fixture in Kosovo on Thursday, a match overshadowed in the build-up by the Israel games.Asked whether the far from ideal preparation for Sunday's game would affect the players, the Irish boss said "we will see"."Nobody is comfortable but it's about limiting the damage, both personally and for Irish football, that we need to find some solution on it," Hallgrimsson added."There is no action we do that everyone will agree to, so we need to find a solution to limit the damage for us as a group, for Ireland as a nation and the association for football in Ireland."We don't know the consequences if we don't play the game but a lot of players share a common feeling, so there are two choices and both are tough. It's a situation you can't win."A spokesperson for the Irish governement insists any decision regarding the fixtures lie firmly at the door of the FAI and Uefa."The FAI had decided to play the fixtures against Israel in accordance with their obligations as members of Uefa. Following engagement with players today decision stands," they said."The FAI has strongly represented the views of its membership that Israel should be excluded from international football competitions, including bringing a motion to Uefa to this effect last year. The reality is that this motion was not passed by Uefa and that the FAI was obliged to fulfil the fixture."Israel Football Association [IFA] head of communications Shlomi Barzel commended the Republic of Ireland team for confirming they will play, saying "football has won".Barzel began Israel's news conference with a statement before requesting  questions regarding the game-only were directed towards captain Dor Peretz and head coach Ran Ben-Shimon who remained on script."The separation between football and politics must be maintained, any other approach spell chaos," he said, confirming Israel players intend to shake hands before the game."The Irish football association [FAI] and the national team players did he right thing by recognising this, even if it took a bit longer than it should. Yet, it is better to be late than never."The one who certainly lost today are those who want to intimidate to separate and turn the football pitch into a political arena. Uefa, the IFA [Israel Football and the FAI stood strong together to prevent it."Barzel also confirmed the IFA intend to appeal both yellow cards shown to Sayed Abu Farhi in Thursday's 3-1 defeat by Austria.Abu Farhi was shown a second yellow for his goal celebration which Barzel insists was not mimicking the firing of a gun, but an "imitation of a snooker player, like the legendary Ken Doherty."

schema.headline: Israel v Republic of Ireland: Republic of Ireland to wear black armbands for Israel game

title: England embrace chaos - but Spain show it never claims big prizes
description: Thomas Tuchel talked about England having to "embrace the chaos" as they embarked on recovery from the crushing disappointment of World Cup semi-final
body: Thomas Tuchel talked about England having to "embrace the chaos" as they embarked on recovery from the crushing disappointment of World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina.As England took those first steps on the road to rehabilitation against reigning world and European champions Spain in the Nations League at Wembley, head coach Tuchel learned the brutal lesson that chaos without control is a loser's strategy at elite level.Spain do control, not chaos. And this is why they are serial winners and England remain a nearly team without a major men's success since the 1966 World Cup.England delivered moments to admire in the 3-2 defeat, even embracing those chaotic spells in an enthralling encounter, but ultimately they came up short once more against this summer's World Cup winners, who are now unbeaten in 39 games.Once Tuchel's England stopped playing themselves into trouble by mimicking Spain's passing style without having anywhere near the quality of their opponents and followed their own "DNA", to use the buzz-phrase of the moment, they actually threatened with power and pace.Quite how England reached the 36th minute only one goal down was a mystery to everyone inside Wembley, Marc Guehi's inexplicable turn into trouble gifting Lamine Yamal an opener inside two minutes.Ferran Torres saw a goal ruled out for offside, was denied by a fine stop by England goalkeeper James Trafford, then rolled an effort wide of the post when clean through.England took advantage of those reprieves to somehow be ahead by the break, through star performer Anthony Gordon's composed finish and Harry Kane's deflected header.Kane's penalty miss just after the break was a turning point, hitting the bar after slipping and touching the ball twice, before England once again paid the price for errors.Nico O'Reilly coughed up possession in the build-up to Alex Baena's equaliser before another substitute in Mikel Oyarzabal, who scored the winner in the Euro 2024 final against England in Berlin, settled matters after 74 minutes.If it was a bad night for Manchester City defensive duo Guehi and O'Reilly, it was not much better for Jarell Quansah, who was given the nod ahead of the recalled Trent Alexander-Arnold. He was uncertain throughout and does not look a natural right-back - perhaps because he is not a natural right-back.Of course, it could have been different had Kane scored his penalty. He did not and it was not.Kane said: "On another day we could have won." This was not another day and England did not win.England's bolder approach after a shaky opening 25 minutes offered up the prospect of a landmark victory, but shambolic defending saw Guehi and O'Reilly present gifts Spain were happy to accept.As against Argentina in the World Cup semi-final in Atlanta, England led by a Gordon goal and lost, but at least here they went down swinging and not by going into cowering retreat.It was a small mercy appreciated by the home support, but the gulf in class when it mattered was still evident as Spain's smooth, unhurried style cut a sharp contrast to England's often frantic efforts.Tuchel's defence looked horribly vulnerable and easy to slice through, although keeper Trafford – given two games before first-choice Jordan Pickford returns – was blameless and will have created a good impression as he tries to create greater competition in that department.They have now shipped 13 goals in their last six matches in all competitions, after conceding only seven in their first 17 games under Tuchel.Ironically, it was two players now plying their trade in Spain, Gordon at Barcelona and Jude Bellingham at Real Madrid, who were England's standout performers.Gordon was in electrifying form, while Bellingham was relentless in driving England forward, even in a losing cause.As for the chaos, Tuchel begged to differ.He told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I'm not sure there was a lot of chaos. We had an incredible amount of high-ball recoveries in the opponent's half. I think 15 more than Spain. Overall, I think 15 in total in the first half. That only goes against a team like Spain if we play man to man, so we were very brave."Tuchel added: "The defending and the deep block were excellent, except for the third goal where we got cut open through the middle. This normally should not happen. "Offensively, I think we played in a clear structure. We tried to switch sides a lot. We tried to put the full-backs up to make the difference and they did. A lot of good stuff but unfortunately not the result."On the gap between the sides, Tuchel said: "We saw no gap except for the technical execution. In the last 20 metres, they were superior than us."Tuchel's comments are questionable here, ignoring the fact that if Spain's own technical execution was better they could easily have been four goals up before England scored, but he was correct to point out the improvement after Gordon drew them level.England captain Kane said: "I spoke before that we reached good levels at the World Cup but didn't quite put a full 90 minutes together. It was probably similar again here. We had a couple of good moments though, that period was as good as we've played in a long, long time and that's the standard we know we can reach."We're playing against the world champions, the European champions, and we went toe-to-toe. On another day for sure we'd have won that game."England certainly embrace the chaos, as Tuchel suggested, but chaos alone does not claim big prizes and never has.At least this is a lesson Tuchel did not have to wait too long to learn after the World Cup.

schema.headline: England embrace chaos - but Spain show it never claims big prizes

title: Why bookshops are booming in the TikTok age
description: Opening your own book shop might be a lofty daydream for some bookworms looking to escape their 9-5, but more and more people are making it a reality.
body: Opening your own book shop might be a lofty daydream for some bookworms looking to escape their 9-5, but more and more people are making it a reality.According to the Booksellers Association, the number of independent book shops in the UK and Ireland is now at its highest level since 2012, with 1,086 stores in 2025 - up from a record low of 867 in 2016.But what is the reality of life as a small bookseller, competing with Amazon, finding new customers, and actually trying to make a profit?Sally Flint, 57, opened The Book Stop in Brigg, North Lincolnshire, just six weeks ago.So far, the "dream" move is living up to her expectations, but it has not been without its challenges. "It's brilliant. It's just like it's Christmas Day every day, because you're just with other people who love books and love reading," she says.However, to make her dream possible, Sally is working up to 14 hours a day.She describes her first foray into bookselling as a "steep learning curve", but says she is having "lots of fun along the way".

schema.headline: Why bookshops are booming in the TikTok age

title: Orange Order successfully challenge injuction banning Drumcree parade
description: Controversial Orange Order march to go ahead for first time in nearly 30 years after late night dramaImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The para
body: Controversial Orange Order march to go ahead for first time in nearly 30 years after late night dramaImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The parade (pictured above in 2018 on a 20th anniversary protest) had been halted due to a temporary injunction being granted at the High Court in Belfast.ByDeclan HarveyUpdated 19 minutes agoA controversial Orange Order parade is set to go ahead in a nationalist part of Northern Ireland after nearly 30 years.Following a series of legal challenges, the High Court ruled in the early hours of Sunday that the initial decision by the Parades Commission had to be respected.The Drumcree parade, which in the 1990s sparked some of the most serious disorder in Northern Ireland's history, had been given permission to go ahead along the Garvaghy Road in Portadown with restrictions in place.However, that decision was challenged in several different courts in Belfast on Saturday before finally being given the go ahead just hours before the parade is due to take place.Image caption, DUP MP Carla Lockhart and loyalist activist Jamie Bryson address the media after the final court rulingFigure caption, A large crowd gathered on the Garvaghy Road late on Saturday night, after appeal court judges overturned an earlier court injunction temporarily banning the marchReaction to final court rulingThe Orange Order, is the most prominent of the loyal orders associated with Protestants in Northern Ireland.Speaking outside court Democratic Unionist MP Carla Lockhart described the decision allowing the parade to go ahead as a "seismic night for the rule of law".The Upper Bann representative added: "This is not a night to be triumphant"Loyalist activist Jamie Bryson, who has acted as a legal adviser for Portadown district lodge, said:"We look to chief constable to make sure this parade is policed.""We will march peacefully, respectfully and lawfully."However Sinn Féin MP John Finucane said the decision had left Garvaghy Road residents feeling" angry and scared""They have a right to feel like that," he said. "We have and we will stand with residents of Garvaghy Road"A large crowd gathered on the Garvaghy Road in the wake of an appeal court ruling which overturned a High Court judge issuing a temporary ban on the parade.Masked men also blocked the north end of the Garvaghy Road, towards Drumcree.Reacting to the Court of Appeal ruling Breandan Mac Cionnaith of the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition said: "There's no such thing as justice or rights for our community. I'm going back to help defend my community."Sínn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald and Stormont First Minister Michelle O'Neill also pledged to "stands fully with the Garvaghy Road community".A day of drama unfolded at Laganside courts after a High Court judge issued an injunction banning the Orange Order parade overturning the Parades Commission decision.The move came after Portadown District Orange Lodge declined Judge Patricia Smyth's request to postpone the parade until all issues were properly considered.What is the Garvaghy Road dispute all about?This was later successfully challenged by an Orange Order member at the Court of Appeal.Towards midnight the Garavaghy Road Residents Coalition was given permission to challenge the decision at the High Court where Mr Justice Humphreys upheld the ruling.'Potential to escalate'The basis of the High Court review was on the PSNI's risk assessment to the Parades Commission.Lawyer Denise Kiley KC for the residents told the court hearing that "much remains uncertain" in the wake of the ruling.She claimed that "nowhere" in the PSNI's contribution to the commission was there "any assessment of future risk" and was "entirely directed to past risk"."That all leads to a requirement for more time and for the Parades Commission to explain the discrepancy that is apparent on the face of the documents," she said.Delivering her decision to issue an injuction, Judge Smyth said "the level of mistrust" between residents and the lodge cannot be "overstated.""It is also clear to me that this particular long running dispute has the potential to escalate within Northern Ireland," she added."Against that backdrop I am thoroughly of the view the issues of all three parties must be properly ventilated."Afterwards GRRC spokesperson Breandan Mac Cionnaith said that "this isn't over yet".He told supporters in a crowd of several hundred outside the High Court not to be "triumphalist".But, he added, "we're halfway there".Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Breandan Mac Cionnaith outside the High Court on SaturdayReacting to developments DUP leader Gavin Robinson MP said unionists would await the appeal court's decision and expect "all parties to respect the legal process"."The Orangemen of Portadown have conducted themselves with dignity and respect for the rule of law for 28 years. If they must wait for further deliberation, be it 28 days, they will do so with their heads held high and dignity intact."SDLP leader Claire Hanna MP said Drumcree "carries a history and a meaning that cannot be ignored". "I welcome that the heat has been taken out of this difficult episode. Lighting the tinder is easy; putting the fire out is much harder."Alliance deputy leader Eóin Tennyson MLA, said that calm heads were needed."Following the High Court's intervention, it is important that everyone now takes a step back and responds responsibly," he said.'Step back from the abyss'Earlier on Saturday Judge Smyth had given the parties involved a final opportunity to "reach an agreement" and "step back from the abyss".Judge Smyth said "it is my view the issues at stake are so sensitive and so important, I would expect all of the lawyers to be creative and to use the law for the good of all the people in Northern Ireland."The judge said the issue the court is dealing with is of "fundamental importance" to the entire society in Northern Ireland.Portadown District Lodge submitted a letter in which they outlined their reasons for not agreeing to delay the parade."The suggestion there is no prejudice to us is, to be frank, absolutely contrary to all reality," the letter said."The prejudice is very clear – those opposed to us could simply ramp up the threat of disorder or violence, to change the factual context, and therefore effectively act as a veto."It added: "This is not balanced or fair to us; it is depriving us, potentially on a permanent basis, of what we have been lawfully granted for Sunday, with no guarantee this outcome will be replicated even if the Applicant's case is ultimately found to be without any merit whatsoever."The letter concluded: "We would ask the court not to take this unprecedented and extraordinary step, which we are advised is unheard of and has hitherto not ever occurred."Image source, PA MediaImage caption, The Parades Commission has determined that the parade can depart Drumcree Parish Church no later than 08:00 BST on SundayEarlier the judge highlighted that the information provided to the court from the PSNI has "promoted further enquiries" and "further time would be of benefit to the court.""In my view it would be contrary to justice and unwise to proceed to make a decision in the absence of information in relation to the issues I have identified."She said the important date for the Orange Order was July 5 and therefore there "is no prejudice in adjourning for a short period to allow this case to be prepared by all parties ."Rather than start at 13:00 BST on Sunday as intended, the Parades Commission had said the march could depart no later than 08:00 and with 35 participants , externalrather than the 60 the Orange Order requested. No bands or supporters are allowed.According to the Drumcree Catholic Church parish website, external, Mass takes place at 08:30 on Sundays in the church of St John the Baptist on the Garvaghy Road. When asked by BBC News NI if Mass time had been taken into consideration, the Parades Commission said commissioners "recognise that the timings set out in the determination" should allow the church service "to proceed as normal".Image source, Catholic Communications Office archiveImage caption, Archbishop Eamon Martin said his thoughts were with those affected by the situation 'March going to clash with Massgoers'In a statement on Saturday afternoon Archbishop Eamon Martin called for "prayers and support for a peaceful resolution to complex Garvaghy Road situation".The Catholic primate said he shared the "sense of shock and disappointment of so many people at recent developments"."I also appeal for support for the patient use of solely lawful and democratic processes to resolve this deeply complex and emotive situation."Fr Peter Clarke, from St John the Baptist in Portadown, said he was concerned the march would "clash" with parishioners coming and going from the church.He said he had emailed the commission to express his concerns and stated he "doesn't know how they came to" their conclusion.Parishioners at St Patrick's Church on William Street are also likely to be affected ahead of the 10:00 service, according to the priest.He added "tensions are high" in the community, and said he will be addressing the situation during Sunday's service.The decision to give the go-ahead for the parade came after the five-person Parades Commission, led by Prof Evelyn Collins, held face-to-face talks with the Orange Order earlier this week, and a separate meeting with the residents' coalition.Senior police officers were also consulted about the planned parade.Within the 31-paragraph determination by the Parades Commission, details were revealed of conversations held with the PSNI.The document stated: "The police made both written and oral submissions, indicating that they, at the time of making them, had no information indicating that the parade would result in disorder or violence."The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) said it had activated "mutual aid arrangements to support contingency planning for a policing operation" in Portadown on Sunday.It is understood about 200 officers are coming from Scotland.When did the Drumcree dispute begin?Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, British soldiers erect a security fence at Drumcree Church in July 2002The Parades Commission has been in the political spotlight since its previous Drumcree determination was quashed in the High Court in August.A review of the commission has since been ordered by the Northern Ireland Office.The Drumcree parade dispute began in the mid-1990s and it almost derailed the peace process at the time.Violence related to the dispute resulted in riots, roadblocks and murders.When the Orange Order was prevented by police from walking down the route in July 1995 there was a tense stand-off. It was the same for the next three years.The Parades Commission began operating in 1998 to regulate parades and try to defuse tension around marches.Its decision not to allow a march down the Garvaghy Road that summer has been challenged by the order over the past three decades.

schema.headline: Orange Order successfully challenge injuction banning Drumcree parade

title: Budget 2026: The two big calls Chancellor John Healey has to make
description: "It is tough," John Healey admitted to me earlier this month when I asked him if there had been too much doom-mongering?"Conflicts, uncertainty, drivi
body: "It is tough," John Healey admitted to me earlier this month when I asked him if there had been too much doom-mongering?"Conflicts, uncertainty, driving up inflation, driving up interest rates. But we've got great strengths. We've got good reasons to be confident about the future of Britain," he insisted.The new scheme to try and help young people get on the property ladder, announced on Saturday, was aimed at boosting confidence in the economy.But the chancellor is now facing two big decisions before his inaugural Budget on 28 October.Firstly, about the longevity of the economic pressures caused by the Iran War, and then about how to sustain a modest but notable uptick in economic spirits, through yet more global turbulence.In his first weeks as chancellor the oil price fell as low as $75 a barrel while the yield - the effective interest rate - on 10-year government bonds was 4.9%.Just over two months later oil has largely traded above $100 and the 10-year yield is at around 5.4%. It is the ultimate double whammy for a chancellor facing his first Budget.Yet there is something unusual about this energy shock. It could quickly reverse, as illustrated earlier in the summer when assumptions about a deescalation in the US Iran conflict led to sharp falls in energy prices and yields.In New York this week both President Trump and his Iranian counterpart President Pezeshkian suggested November's US midterm elections were connected to when the war might end.The Iranians would wait until after the elections to seek peace because the war's impact on the cost of living - particularly soaring diesel costs - could damage him electorally, the US president told the UN General Assembly.The Iranian president said his nation "didn't want it to get to the midterms".Both sides in this war are feeling the economic squeeze of conflict. The 3 November vote is six days after the Budget. No one could rely on there being a settlement by then, but it is plausible.So the Budget tax, spend and borrowing forecasts could be based on a prolonged conflict, which is actually on the cusp of ending, or even already ended. The chancellor has to therefore decide whether to plan for the worst, and make some painful permanent tax and spend decisions, or buy some time.One option is to let borrowing take some of the strain, by tolerating a reduction in the £24bn of headroom - room for manoeuvre against its self-imposed borrowing rules - left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves.This year's headroom will be judged in three years rather than four, so there is some rationale as to why a smaller number over a closer target might be appropriate.And while higher inflation means higher interest costs, it also means higher cash tax receipts, at a time when thresholds continue to be frozen.There is a second consideration. The hopeful optimism "vibes" strategy of the Burnham administration appears to have had some impact.The longest running UK consumer confidence survey has hit a two-year high. Among younger people it has not been this high since before Brexit.Some data companies call it a "Burnham bounce", although the weather and World Cup were also factors.There is evidence, more mixed, that business optimism has also perked up in recent months, possibly because of earlier falls in energy prices, though this has been clouded by anticipation of possible tax rises. Business group, the Institute of Directors said this was despite, rather than because of, the new government.While no one should get too carried away with these turnarounds, they do stand in contrast to the admitted mistake of the Starmer government in talking up consumer pain, two years ago. The question for the chancellor is whether better consumer and business spirits can be reconciled with the need for a "challenging" Budget?Indeed, it's important to determine how much of the summer global bond market shock is solely down to the impact of the Iran war and how much is more structural.Governments are facing new and intense competition in bond markets from the world's biggest AI businesses. In addition, the UK has had recent, prominent political and economic uncertainty.Right now the bond markets are like a pack of wolves stalking red deer, probing for weaknesses."At times like this you don't want to be at the back of the herd," said one very senior former Treasury adviser. In response, the Treasury has pointed to the UK having the highest growth and the fastest falling borrowing of the major G7 countries so far this year and our overall energy prices starting to decouple from high and volatile gas prices.However, the IMF chief Kristalina Georgieva this week dismissed the idea that advanced nations could pause their fiscal homework, while the Gulf situation calmed."Bring debt levels down, make fiscal consolidation as a priority… it is impossible to stress strongly enough how critical it is to get the courage to take the steps that are necessary," Georgieva told me, acknowledging the UK's "fairly consistent, credible" plans.Then there is the curious conundrum of British productivity. Last year, the government's official forecaster the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) downgraded the UK's productivity peformance, leading to a notable hit to the public finances.Now the UK's productivity record has been upgraded materially by the Office for National Statistics, although this is because of fewer hours worked. There could therefore be an argument to reverse some of that downgrade.Separately, the new chair of the OBR Jonathan Haskel is known for his argument that official statistics understate investment in intangibles like software and data. His latest research suggests AI-related investment is already visible in US productivity figures, and he has long been optimistic about tech's impact on the future.While it seems unlikely that such factors will make it into the OBR's calculations next month, there is a real debate here. Officially, however, part of the job at the Budget is to identify cuts to fund the Defence Investment Plan, inherited from Sir Keir. That's before funding the additional move to 3% of GDP and a new social care system. Even a promise of less welfare spending looks like being built on an upfront investment in jobs for young people.One change from last year is that so far, the government has parked the "pitch-rolling" with a silence that would rival the Trappist monks.Instead, policy announcements are strategically timed such as the "Your First Home" scheme just as the Labour party conference got underway. We can expect to hear plenty more as the Budget nears.

schema.headline: Budget 2026: The two big calls Chancellor John Healey has to make

title: Andy Burnham announces scheme to help first-time buyers
description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham is to introduce a new scheme to try to help young people get on the property ladder.The "Your First Home" scheme would be
body: Prime Minister Andy Burnham is to introduce a new scheme to try to help young people get on the property ladder.The "Your First Home" scheme would be open to first-time buyers in England with a deposit of 2.5%. It would provide them with a loan worth 20% of their new build property's value to help pay for the purchase.Burnham said people who do not have support from the "bank of mum and dad" are among those the scheme would aim to help.There would be an initial interest-free period for the equity loan, with more details expected in next month's Budget.The Conservatives warned the policy would leave first-time buyers taking on more debt and risks "pushing up the price of new homes".Burnham said: "Too many young people are struggling with the cost of housing, with many giving up hope of ever having a home to call their own."So we will step in to help more first-time buyers on to the housing ladder."The PM added he believes the scheme will give builders the "confidence to deliver the high-quality new homes the country needs".Funding for the scheme is expected to come from reprioritising existing budgets, but housing developers will pay towards the running costs.Ministers have not yet confirmed whether there is an age restriction on the scheme, or a cap on the price on the value of the property.The policy is similar to initiatives from previous governments, including the coalition's Help To Buy scheme, introduced in 2013 by then-Chancellor George Osborne.It expanded a previous scheme, known as FirstBuy, which was aimed solely at first-time buyers.Help to Buy initially enabled all purchasers to put down a 5% deposit on a newly built home, with a value of up to a £600,000.Up to 20% of the cost of the home was funded by a shared equity loan, which was interest-free for the first five years.The first version of the programme was active until 2021. A second iteration of the scheme, which ran until 2023, restricted access to first-time buyers and applied regional-level price caps to the properties that could be bought.An evaluation of the scheme, external found more than 387,000 properties were purchased through it, of which 328,000 were by first-time buyers.In its conclusion, the report noted Help to Buy was "effective in supporting people into home ownership in some areas, but did not remove affordability barriers for first-time buyers in areas that were already relatively expensive".Housing Secretary Angela Rayner said "Your First Home" would "build on the lessons learned from previous schemes, while retaining the benefits".The Home Builders Federation welcomed the proposals, saying it had "long called for action to improve access to home ownership"."Our analysis shows a well-designed scheme can make a meaningful difference for households struggling to get on to the property ladder," it added.Conservative shadow housing secretary Katie Lam accused Labour of wanting first-time buyers to "take on even more debt to afford the few homes that have been built".She added taxpayers would take a "stake in their homes" and be "picking up the bill for months".Lam said: "Slapping another levy on developers risks pushing up the price of new homes too. "This is a colossal admission of failure. This Labour government is making homes harder to build, then asking buyers to borrow more to pay for them."Lam said the Conservatives want to scrap stamp duty, "back British house builders" and ensure that houses are "built in the places that people actually want to live".Rayner told the BBC earlier this month that there was only a "slim chance" the government would meet its target of building 1.5m homes in England by the next election, but said she was "not giving it up".Data up to June this year suggested the government was behind on the rate of construction needed to meet the goal, which housebuilders have previously warned was too optimistic.BBC Verify analysis showed a decline in the number of new houses being built during Labour's first year in power - continuing a fall that began under the Conservatives.The housing policy announcement came as Burnham arrived in Liverpool ahead of his first Labour Party conference since becoming prime minister.The PM said he wanted to make it a "really important week where we set out a new direction for the country".He added: "We've had a decade since Brexit and it's been a decade of too much drift, too much division, and we need to draw a line on that."Another pre-conference announcement included a pledge to offer quicker access of a guaranteed job to young people receiving health or disability support.The offer would be made three months after they start claiming benefits. This approach would be introduced from next April.Labour said the government would cover 100% of wage costs for up to 25 hours a week for six months.Currently, jobless young people aged 18 to 24 must have been on universal credit for 18 months before receiving an offer under the government's job guarantee scheme.Conservative shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said Labour should have cut "burdens" on businesses to help ensure disabled people are employed.She said: "Instead, they are bringing back a Conservative post-pandemic scheme. Andy Burnham clearly has no new ideas."Whately also questioned how the change would be funded.

schema.headline: Andy Burnham announces scheme to help first-time buyers

title: Time running out for Tennessee killer Christa Pike who says she's too damaged for death row
description: Christa Pike to be first woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years - but her defence say she's a victim tooImage source, Tennesse Department of Correct
body: Christa Pike to be first woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years - but her defence say she's a victim tooImage source, Tennesse Department of CorrectionsImage caption, Christa Pike's lawyers have filed a clemency petition seeking to commute her sentence ahead of the 30 September execution date ByStephanie HegartyBBC World Service CorrespondentAshlee Sellars last heard from her friend Christa Pike earlier this week, when Pike texted her from her cell on death row as she prepares to be killed by lethal injection by the US state of Tennessee.Pike told Sellars she does not want any of her loved ones to be present on Wednesday when she is executed. "She doesn't want us to experience that," Sellars says.Sellars finds it hard to reconcile this woman, whom she has only known to be kind and protective, with the person who committed a heinous crime 31 years ago.Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995 when Colleen was found with a pentagram, a symbol of Satanic ritual, carved into her chest.Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.A year later she was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Now, after years of failed appeals, Pike's execution has been set for Wednesday. If it goes ahead, she will be the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men.Colleen's mother has said she wants Pike's execution to happen so that her daughter "finally can be resting".Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Student Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed in the 1995 murderBut Pike's lawyers, who filed a 226-page clemency petition, are still hoping for a last-minute reprieve, and UN human rights experts have also called for the execution to be stopped., external Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence.In the years since her sentencing, her defence team have uncovered details about her childhood that they say the jury never had the chance to consider."It is mind-boggling that they did not present any of her history of abuse and rape, even though they knew about it," says Sandra Babcock, an expert in gender and the death penalty at Cornell Law School, who has worked on Pike's defence."Her case is so uniquely compelling, not just because of her really incomprehensible history of sexual violence but the combination of that with her youth and her mental illness."Image source, Christa PikeImage caption, Christa Pike suffered neglect and was abused by her parentsIn 1995, forensic psychologist Dr Diana McCoy was hired by Pike's defence team and found she was severely neglected by both of her parents. McCoy's report found Pike was physically and sexually abused by several of her mother's husbands and boyfriends, and raped several times, once when she was 11 and again aged 17. Later it was discovered that she was repeatedly raped as a toddler by her grandmother's boyfriend. McCoy said Pike's mother didn't believe her that these rapes happened.But Pike's trial lawyer did not put McCoy on the stand or call many of the witnesses she recommended. These details emerged more than a decade later in a court hearing reviewing her case, when a new team of lawyers claimed ineffective assistance of counsel, a claim that was denied by the judge.In 2021 Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder in prison and has been medicated since.Later, another forensic psychologist working for Pike's defence, Dr Bethany Brand, who assessed Pike in 2023, said her case was extremely rare because she was abused by so many people who should have protected her."Her childhood was replete with physical, sexual, and emotional abuse. She was sexually violated by a number of men, starting before she was school age," she says.Brand says Pike had untreated manic episodes due to bipolar disorder and untreated PTSD. "Both of those things together absolutely influenced how threatened she felt by the girl she ended up killing and her lack of emotional control in that situation."Babcock adds: "If they let her be executed, then what it tells us is that the death penalty in this country is just a joke. It's not for the worst of the worst. It is for the people who receive the worst legal representation and who are the most damaged and vulnerable."Image source, Christa PikeImage caption, Pike, pictured as a teenager, killed Slemmer in January 1995 after telling a friend she "just felt mean that day", court documents say'She should pay for it'Last year, Tennessee's Supreme Court ruled Pike had not shown circumstances that would justify commuting her sentence. Her appeals process had been exhausted and a date was set for her execution.A federal appeals court had earlier ruled that the jury had already heard about her difficult childhood during testimony from her mother, father, and aunt during her trial. And that new evidence of bipolar disorder, PTSD, and brain damage "mostly repeated" what the jury had heard and would not have changed the verdict. The row has some parallels with the high-profile case of murderer Lisa Montgomery, whose lawyers also argued she was a mentally ill victim of abuse who deserved mercy.Montgomery's legal challenges failed to commute her sentence, and she was executed by lethal injection in Indiana in 2021.Unless she is granted clemency by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, Pike will be executed on 30 September. That decision is unlikely to come until the last moment, and Lee has never granted clemency in a death penalty case before.The Tennessee Supreme Court this week denied Pike's request to halt the execution. Her counsel say they have been discussing next steps.On her execution day, Pike has requested an all-female team. She says being held down by a group of men will exacerbate her trauma. The state of Tennessee has said the goal is that female guards will transfer Pike to the prison where she will be executed but hasn't guaranteed it.Colleen's mother May Martinez supports Christa's execution."She did the crime. I think she should pay for it," she said on Knoxville TV station WBIR in 2021, and told the BBC this week she still stands by those comments.Pike should suffer before she dies, Martinez told WBIR. "I would feel better that she felt the same pain that Colleen did."Image source, J. Miles Carey/USA TODAY/Imagn Images via ReutersImage caption, May Martinez, mother of Colleen Slemmer, and a retired Knoxville Police department detective outside a courtroom for a post-conviction hearing in 2006"My heart breaks every single day because I keep reliving it and reliving it, and I can't no more, and I want this to happen before I die," she added."There's not a day goes by that I don't think about Colleen or how she died and how rough it was. I just want Christa down so I can end it, relieve my daughter, so she finally can be resting."The Justice Coalition, a victims' rights advocacy group, has raised money to help Martinez travel to Tennessee to watch the execution.The group's executive director, Robert Bracewell, said this sentence was determined by a jury of Pike's peers and it is what Colleen's family want."We stand firm with the family that on the 30 September her execution ought to proceed."Ashlee Sellars grapples with two seemingly conflicting beliefs: that Colleen's mother has a right to feel justice has been served and that everyone, including her friend Christa, deserves a chance at redemption."When I think about reconciling who you see on TV or the horrible tragedy that happened with Colleen, the only thing that makes sense to me is around mental health and trauma and the way that people process stuff in a moment when they don't have the things that they need," Sellars says."These horrible things happen in your youth and then those traumas moved through you, in our community, and you cause harm to somebody else."Sellars met Pike in prison while serving a 25-year sentence for her involvement in a robbery-murder. They spoke to each other through the meal flaps in their doors on the high security unit. Now, Sellars works as an advocate for justice reform and victims of crime."People want to know that everyone's life matters, right? They want to know that Colleen's life mattered," she says."Christa in this moment, I think she is fighting much more for her life to matter than she is to actually live."

schema.headline: Time running out for Tennessee killer Christa Pike who says she's too damaged for death row
